analysis.investment_thesis: Borosil Renewables is India's sole domestic solar glass manufacturer — a structurally interesting niche — but Chinese import dumping has obliterated margins so thoroughly that EBITDA collapsed 72% (₹256 Cr → ₹73 Cr) even as revenue grew 130% from 2022 to 2025. Owning the only factory doesn't matter if you can't price above cost of capital.
key_strengths: Sole domestic solar glass manufacturer — regulatory protection via anti-dumping duties is a credible catalyst
Strong promoter commitment at 58.77% holding with manageable D/E of 0.23x after debt repayment in FY25
India's solar buildout (200 GW target) creates structural demand tailwind over a decade
key_risks: Margin destruction from Chinese imports: EBITDA/revenue collapsed from ~40% (2022) to ~5% (2025) with no floor visible
Chronic negative FCF every year shown (worst: -₹353 Cr in 2023); the business consumes capital rather than generating it
Valuation is disconnected from reality — P/B 5.93x and EV/EBITDA 20x on a business posting -₹87 Cr net loss in FY25
red_flags: ROE -8.90% and ROCE -4.41% — negative returns on capital are the cardinal sin for a Munger-style investor
Net losses accelerating: -₹50 Cr (FY24) → -₹87 Cr (FY25) despite 7.6% revenue growth to ₹1,476 Cr
Finance costs tripled (₹8 Cr → ₹32 Cr) while EBITDA halved — interest coverage is perilously thin at ~2.3x
OCF positive only 3 of 5 years; capex outstripped OCF every single year — growth funded entirely by debt/equity dilution
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Inverting first, as one must: what kills this investment? Chinese manufacturers produce solar glass at a fraction of Borosil's cost, and they have been selling into India at predatory prices. The evidence is in the numbers — revenue grew from ₹642 Cr (FY22) to ₹1,476 Cr (FY25), a 130% jump, yet EBITDA collapsed from ₹256 Cr to ₹73 Cr. That is the signature of a commodity producer with no pricing power, selling more volume at ever-thinner margins. Operating income in FY25 is ₹58 Cr — identical to FY24 — on a cost base that keeps growing. A business that cannot translate revenue growth into earnings growth has no moat worth speaking of.

The capital structure tells the rest of the story. Borosil spent ₹1,047 Cr in capex over 2022–2025 to expand capacity, funded largely by borrowings (debt peaked at ₹576 Cr in FY24). FCF has been negative in every year shown. Now, with losses mounting and debt partially repaid (₹252 Cr by FY25), the company faces a binary outcome: either anti-dumping duties are imposed decisively and margins recover, or losses continue until equity is impaired. At ₹6,987 Cr market cap on -₹87 Cr net profit, the market is pricing in a full recovery with no margin of safety — exactly the kind of speculative, hope-driven pricing I avoid. The only scenario warranting attention is if the government imposes strong, lasting anti-dumping protection, but government policy is not a business model.
